notes:
1. Economic Trends — Meaning

  • Economic trends refer to the direction in which major economic indicators change over time.
  • Important indicators include GSDP, growth, per capita income, sectoral structure, investment, exports, employment, inflation and State finances.
📌 Must-Memorise

Economic Trend → Direction of Change Over Time

2. Trend vs Short-Term Fluctuation

  • A single year's rise or fall does not necessarily establish a long-term trend.
  • Agriculture, for example, may fluctuate because of rainfall while the broader economy continues a long-term structural transformation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

One-Year Performance ≠ Long-Term Economic Trend

3. GSDP — Meaning

  • GSDP stands for Gross State Domestic Product.
  • It represents the value of final goods and services produced within a State during a specified period.
📌 Must-Memorise

GSDP → State-Level Economic Output

4. Tamil Nadu GSDP — 2024–25

According to the supplied Economic Survey:

  • Tamil Nadu's GSDP at current prices reached approximately ₹31.19 lakh crore in 2024–25.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN GSDP 2024–25 → ₹31.19 Lakh Crore

5. Nominal Growth vs Real Growth

  • Nominal growth measures output at current prices.
  • It reflects both:
  • Change in actual production.
  • Change in prices.
  • Real growth adjusts for price changes and better reflects changes in actual production.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Nominal Growth ≠ Real Growth

6. Tamil Nadu Growth — 2024–25

According to the supplied source:

  • Nominal growth → about 16%.
  • Real growth → 11.2%.
  • The State Economic Survey reported this real growth as the highest among major States for 2024–25.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Real Growth 2024–25 → 11.2%

7. Tamil Nadu's Share in India's Economy

  • Tamil Nadu accounted for approximately 9.4% of India's GDP in 2024–25 according to the supplied Economic Survey.
  • This is large relative to the State's share of India's land area and population.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Contribution to India GDP → ~9.4%

8. Economic Diversification

Tamil Nadu's economic strength comes from a combination of:

  • Automobiles.
  • Electronics.
  • Textiles.
  • Leather.
  • Engineering.
  • IT.
  • Financial and business services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diversification → Lower Dependence on One Sector

9. Tamil Nadu Per Capita Income — 2024–25

According to the supplied source:

  • Tamil Nadu per capita income → approximately ₹3.62 lakh.
  • National average → approximately ₹2.05 lakh.
  • Tamil Nadu was about 1.77 times the national average.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Per Capita Income 2024–25 → ₹3.62 Lakh

10. Per Capita Income — Limitation

  • Per capita income measures average economic capacity.
  • It does not directly show:
  • Income distribution.
  • Poverty.
  • Employment quality.
  • Regional inequality.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High Per Capita Income ≠ Equal Distribution

11. Structural Transformation — Meaning

  • Structural transformation refers to the long-term shift in economic importance from agriculture towards industry and services.
  • Tamil Nadu has moved substantially away from an agriculture-dominated structure.

12. Tamil Nadu GSVA Structure — 2024–25

Approximate sector shares:

  • Primary → 13.4%.
  • Secondary → 33.1%.
  • Services → 53.6%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Economy → Services-Led + Strong Industrial Base

13. Primary Sector

The primary sector broadly includes:

  • Agriculture.
  • Livestock.
  • Forestry.
  • Fishing.
  • Its share is smaller than industry and services, though it remains socially important.

14. Secondary Sector

The secondary sector includes:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Electricity and related activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Secondary Sector → Major Tamil Nadu Strength

15. Services Sector

Major services include:

  • Trade.
  • Transport.
  • IT.
  • Finance.
  • Real estate.
  • Tourism.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Professional services.
  • Services form the largest part of Tamil Nadu's economy.

16. Manufacturing Growth — 2024–25

According to the supplied source:

  • Tamil Nadu manufacturing real growth → 14.74%.
  • Cited all-India manufacturing growth → about 4.5%.
  • Average Tamil Nadu manufacturing growth during 2021–22 to 2024–25 → about 9.38%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Manufacturing Growth 2024–25 → 14.74%

17. Major Manufacturing Clusters

Important industrial centres include:

  • Chennai region → Automobiles + electronics.
  • Coimbatore → Engineering + manufacturing.
  • Tiruppur → Knitwear.
  • Hosur → Advanced manufacturing and industrial growth.
  • Ranipet/Ambur → Leather and footwear.

18. Factory Employment

  • The supplied Economic Survey states that Tamil Nadu accounted for approximately 15% of India's factory workforce.
  • This highlights the importance of manufacturing not just for output but also for employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Major Contributor to India's Factory Employment

19. Services Growth — 2024–25

According to the source:

  • Services share of GSVA → 53.6%.
  • Services real growth → approximately 11.3%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Services → Largest Sector + Double-Digit Growth

20. IT and Knowledge Services

  • Chennai is a major IT and business-services centre.
  • Coimbatore is also developing a growing IT and knowledge-services ecosystem.
  • Tamil Nadu's higher-education base supports these activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Education + Skills → Modern Services Expansion

21. Agriculture — Economic Share

  • Agriculture alone contributed approximately 6.6% of State GSVA in 2024–25 according to the supplied source.
  • Its economic share is smaller than industry and services but its livelihood significance remains much larger.

22. Cropped Area and Cropping Intensity

According to the source for 2024–25:

  • Gross cropped area → approximately 62.25 lakh hectares.
  • Cropping intensity → about 1.29.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cropping Intensity > 1 → Same Land Cropped More Than Once on Average

23. Agricultural Productivity Rankings

The supplied Economic Survey reports Tamil Nadu in 2024–25 as:

  • 1st in ragi yield.
  • 1st in sugarcane yield.
  • 2nd in oilseeds.
  • 3rd in groundnut yield.

24. Allied Activities

According to the source:

  • Livestock → about 5.1% of GSVA.
  • Fishing and aquaculture → about 0.99%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rural Economy ≠ Crop Agriculture Alone

25. MSMEs — Economic Role

MSMEs support:

  • Employment.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Supplier networks.
  • Local industrialisation.
  • Regional diversification.

Important areas include:

  • Engineering.
  • Textiles.
  • Food processing.
  • Auto components.
  • Leather.
  • Machinery.
  • Services.

26. Industrial Clusters — Advantage

Clusters reduce costs by providing shared access to:

  • Skilled labour.
  • Suppliers.
  • Logistics.
  • Specialised services.
  • Markets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Cluster → Specialisation + Lower Costs + Employment

27. FDI Trend

According to the supplied source, Tamil Nadu FDI equity inflows rose from:

  • 2022–23 → US$2.169 billion.
  • 2023–24 → US$2.436 billion.
  • 2024–25 → US$3.681 billion.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN FDI Trend → Rising

28. Investment Quality

Investment creates stronger development effects when it generates:

  • Production.
  • Employment.
  • Technology transfer.
  • Local supplier linkages.
  • Export capability.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Investment Value Alone ≠ Development Success

29. Merchandise Export Growth

Tamil Nadu's merchandise exports increased from:

  • 2020–21 → about US$26.15 billion.
  • 2024–25 → about US$52.07 billion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Merchandise Exports Nearly Doubled

30. Export Rankings — 2024–25

According to the supplied source, Tamil Nadu ranked:

  • 1st → Electronics exports.
  • 1st → Textiles exports.
  • 1st → Leather-product exports.
  • 2nd → Engineering exports.
  • 3rd → Total exports.

31. Electronics — Emerging Driver

  • Electronics has become a major new export driver.
  • This indicates movement from traditional manufacturing towards higher-technology production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Traditional Manufacturing → Advanced Manufacturing Shift

32. Export Preparedness and External Risk

  • Tamil Nadu ranked 2nd in the Export Preparedness Index cited by the source.
  • Greater export integration also increases exposure to:
  • Global recessions.
  • Tariff changes.
  • Supply-chain disruptions.

33. Employment Trends

According to the State Economic Survey measure:

  • LFPR → 71.5% in 2021–22.
  • LFPR → 72.1% in 2023–24.
  • Unemployment rate → 5.1% to 3.5% over the same period.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Employment Figures Must Always Be Read with Their Specific Survey Definition

34. Structural Change in Employment

Workers have gradually shifted from agriculture towards:

  • Manufacturing.
  • Construction.
  • Services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Transformation → Agriculture → Industry + Services

35. Employment Quality and Gender Challenge

  • Economic growth must increasingly create:
  • Productive jobs.
  • Formal jobs.
  • Secure employment.
  • Better opportunities for women and youth.
  • The source identifies care responsibilities, mobility and job availability as important constraints on women's employment.

36. Polycentric Urban Growth

Tamil Nadu's economy is distributed across several major centres:

  • Chennai.
  • Coimbatore.
  • Tiruppur.
  • Madurai.
  • Tiruchirappalli.
  • Salem.
  • Hosur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Growth → Multi-Centre, Not Chennai Alone

37. District-Level Income

  • The supplied Economic Survey reports that 32 of 38 districts had per capita income above the all-India average in 2023–24.
  • District disparities nevertheless remain.

38. Industrial Corridors

  • According to the source, all 38 districts are covered by one or more industrial-corridor projects.
📌 Must-Memorise

Policy Direction → Chennai-Centred Growth to Distributed Regional Growth

39. Infrastructure as a Growth Driver

Tamil Nadu's growth is supported by:

  • Roads.
  • Ports.
  • Airports.
  • Industrial corridors.
  • Power infrastructure.
  • Urban transport.
  • Logistics.

40. Capital Expenditure

According to the supplied source:

  • Total capital expenditure from 2020–21 to 2025–26 → approximately ₹2.54 lakh crore.
  • 2025–26 Budget capital expenditure → ₹57,231 crore.
  • This represented a 22.4% increase over the 2024–25 Revised Estimate.

41. Capital Formation — Growth Link

Infrastructure investment generates:

  • Short-term construction demand.
  • Long-term productivity improvements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Capital Formation → Productive Capacity → Future Growth

42. Credit–Deposit Ratio

  • Tamil Nadu recorded a credit–deposit ratio of approximately 120.5% in the comparison cited by the source.
  • It ranked second among States in that comparison.
📌 Must-Memorise

Credit–Deposit Ratio → Credit Relative to Deposits

43. Agricultural Credit

Agricultural credit disbursement increased from:

  • 2019–20 → approximately ₹2.23 lakh crore.
  • 2023–24 → approximately ₹4.52 lakh crore.
  • Around 78% of the relevant farmer loan accounts were reported as belonging to small and marginal farmers.

44. Financial Deepening — Caution

  • Greater credit can support agriculture, MSMEs, housing and investment.
  • But a very high credit–deposit ratio is not automatically positive.
  • Credit quality and repayment capacity also matter.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

More Credit ≠ Automatically Better Credit

45. Inflation Trend

According to the supplied source:

  • 2023–24 → about 5.4%.
  • 2024–25 → about 4.6%.
  • 2025–26 up to December 2025 → about 2.3%.

For the same 2025–26 period:

  • Urban → 2.5%.
  • Rural → 2.1%.

46. Inflation and Real Income

  • Inflation reduces purchasing power.
  • If income rises more slowly than prices, real purchasing power falls.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nominal Income Growth ≠ Real Income Growth

47. State Fiscal Trends

Important indicators include:

  • Revenue receipts.
  • Revenue expenditure.
  • Capital expenditure.
  • Revenue deficit.
  • Fiscal deficit.
  • Public debt.

48. Revenue Deficit — 2025–26

  • The supplied 2025–26 Budget estimated the revenue deficit at approximately ₹41,635 crore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue Deficit → Revenue Expenditure Exceeds Revenue Receipts

49. Fiscal Deficit — 2025–26

According to the source:

  • Fiscal deficit → approximately 3.00% of GSDP.
  • 2024–25 Revised Estimate → 3.26%.
📌 Must-Memorise

TN Fiscal Deficit 2025–26 Budget Estimate → 3.00% of GSDP

50. Tamil Nadu's Fiscal Challenge

The State must simultaneously finance:

  • Welfare.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Salaries.
  • Pensions.
  • Debt servicing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fiscal Goal → Social Expenditure + Productive Investment + Debt Sustainability

51. Social-Sector Expenditure

According to the supplied source:

  • 2021–22 → approximately ₹1,13,268 crore.
  • 2025–26 Revised Estimate → approximately ₹1,57,864 crore.

52. Education and Skill Infrastructure

The source reports for 2024–25:

  • Engineering and architecture colleges → 463.
  • Polytechnic colleges → 492.
  • Higher-education GER → approximately 47%.
📌 Must-Memorise

Large Technical-Education Base → Supports Industry + Services

53. Social Policy as Economic Infrastructure

Investment in:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Mobility.

can increase productive capacity.

📌 Must-Memorise

Human Development → Human Capital → Productivity → Growth

54. Tamil Nadu Growth Model

Tamil Nadu's recent model can broadly be described as:

Strong Manufacturing

  • Large Services Sector
  • Export Growth
  • Investment
  • Human Capital
  • Infrastructure

55. Employment — Future Challenge

Future growth must increasingly generate:

  • Quality jobs.
  • Youth employment.
  • Women's employment.
  • Graduate employment.
  • Formalisation.
  • Skill matching.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High GSDP Growth ≠ Automatic High-Quality Employment

56. Agriculture and Climate Risk

Important agricultural risks include:

  • Rainfall variability.
  • Groundwater stress.
  • Climate change.
  • Post-harvest losses.

Future priorities include:

  • Climate-smart agriculture.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Value addition.

57. Urban Infrastructure Challenge

Continued urbanisation will increase demand for:

  • Housing.
  • Transport.
  • Water.
  • Waste management.
  • Energy.
  • Climate-resilient infrastructure.

58. Global Trade and Technological Change

Tamil Nadu faces both opportunities and risks from:

  • Global supply chains.
  • Trade barriers.
  • Automation.
  • Artificial intelligence.
  • Advanced manufacturing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Technology → Productivity Gains + Changing Skill Demand

59. Fiscal Space — Future Constraint

  • Future development requires adequate resources for both:
  • Social investment.
  • Capital investment.
  • Pensions, pay revisions and recurring commitments can reduce fiscal space.

60. US$1 Trillion Economy Goal

  • Tamil Nadu has articulated the goal of becoming a US$1 trillion economy by 2030.
  • This is a policy target, not the present size of the economy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

US$1 Trillion → 2030 Target

Not Current GSDP

61. TNPSC Traps

  • GSDP and GSVA are related but not identical.
  • Nominal growth and real growth are different.
  • Tamil Nadu GSDP 2024–25 → approximately ₹31.19 lakh crore.
  • Real growth 2024–25 → 11.2%.
  • One high-growth year does not automatically establish a permanent trend.
  • Tamil Nadu share in India's GDP → about 9.4% in the cited 2024–25 source.
  • Per capita income → about ₹3.62 lakh in 2024–25.
  • High per capita income does not mean equal income distribution.
  • Tamil Nadu economy is services-led but has a strong secondary sector.
  • Primary-sector share → 13.4%.
  • Secondary-sector share → 33.1%.
  • Services share → 53.6%.
  • Manufacturing growth → 14.74% in 2024–25.
  • Services growth → about 11.3%.
  • Agriculture's smaller output share does not mean it is socially unimportant.
  • Gross cropped area and net sown area are different.
  • Livestock and fisheries are allied rural activities.
  • MSMEs are important for jobs and local industrial networks.
  • FDI value alone does not measure development impact.
  • Merchandise exports nearly doubled between 2020–21 and 2024–25.
  • Tamil Nadu ranked first in cited electronics, textiles and leather-product exports.
  • Export growth creates global vulnerability as well as opportunity.
  • Employment data must be quoted with its survey definition and year.
  • High growth does not guarantee high-quality employment.
  • Tamil Nadu has a multi-centre urban-industrial structure.
  • State averages can hide district differences.
  • Capital expenditure creates long-term productive assets.
  • High credit–deposit ratio is not automatically good or bad.
  • Inflation reduces real purchasing power.
  • Nominal income growth and real income growth are different.
  • Revenue deficit and fiscal deficit are different.
  • Fiscal deficit cited for 2025–26 Budget → 3.00% of GSDP.
  • Revenue expenditure is not automatically unproductive.
  • Social-sector expenditure can increase human capital.
  • Human capital supports both manufacturing and services.
  • Climate risk can affect agricultural growth.
  • Export orientation increases exposure to international shocks.
  • Automation can raise productivity while changing employment demand.
  • US$1 trillion economy is a 2030 policy target, not the current size.
